justification: Formed a fresh judgement before opening the round-2 review. For the target query 'process vs thread' (CONTENT_PLAN.md section 7, angle C) I fetched the two top-ranking pages. GeeksforGeeks: two non-technical illustrative images, a nine-row comparison table, no runnable code, no measured numbers, no discussion of memory layout, context-switch cost or thread-pool behaviour. ByteByteGo: one unlabelled program->process->thread diagram, ~200 words of explanatory prose, five bullet differences, no code, no quantitative cost data, no crash-isolation or starvation coverage. (Baeldung again returned HTTP 403 and could not be read; Microsoft Learn's own 'About Processes and Threads', which the article also cites as a source, is ~470 words of plain prose with zero diagrams or code, useful only as a lower bound.) Against that bar this article's shell renders 20 real, labelled C# run/Output block pairs, two hand-drawn SVG figures, a clean two-column decision table, and four exercise callouts with collapsed solutions, in a rhythm that alternates prose, code and figures every few paragraphs -- a different order of depth and production value from anything else ranking for this query. I ran node tools/verify-page.mjs --drafts /operating-systems/processes-and-threads/ from PowerShell: FAIL only on the expected placeholder check (NEEDS_MARKUS inside <main>, which is not an issue per the task brief); words=5377, code=20, fig=2, Lighthouse 97/100/100/100, 0 console errors/warnings, 0 broken links (21 external, all resolved), mobileOverflowPx=0. Other agents were active in this repo during the run (see git status on branch batch6-scratch), so the performance sub-score should be treated as indicative rather than final; it is in any case comfortably above the 90 gate and slightly better than round 2's 96. I then opened every desktop-light screenshot (fold + 14 parts) and every mobile-dark screenshot (fold + 22 parts), plus the fold and two interior parts each for desktop-dark and mobile-light -- both figures in all four device/theme combinations. Reading rhythm is well managed: no wall-of-text section runs past a screen or two before a code block, callout or figure breaks it up. Heading hierarchy is clean (single H1, ## for major sections, ### only for 'The private part, measured', which correctly nests under its parent in the TOC). Code blocks never overflow the frame; long lines fade at the right edge with the operative tokens (ProcessorAffinity, WaitOne/Set, Interlocked.Increment, atOnce, {label,-20}) staying inside the visible ~40 columns on phone width, matching WRITER_GUIDE.md section 7. Output panels stay within the same budget. Figure 1 (process/thread address-space box diagram) and Figure 2 (blocked-vs-awaiting thread-pool workers) both use portrait, stacked layouts with annotations placed under each band, exactly per WRITER_GUIDE.md section 5; labels are legible at 390 px in both themes, and the accent/gray/good/bad box classes carry correct semantic colour in dark mode too. The two-column decision table ('Reach for' / 'When you need') never needs horizontal scroll on mobile, and the sources list, exercise blocks and 'Written by' / footer render without incident in every combination checked. Callout variety (note, pitfall, warning, four exercise/solution pairs) is used appropriately and none give away their answer above the fold. As instructed, I then opened round 2's design review (scored 9.0, no blockers or majors) and specifically re-checked the rewritten 'What a context switch costs' paragraph and its surrounding prose against this round's screenshots (desktop-light parts 06-08, mobile-dark parts 09-11, desktop-dark part 10): it still reads as a well-paced sequence of five-to-eight-sentence paragraphs interleaved with one code block and its output, with no overflow, no orphaned headings and no clipped inline code anywhere in that section. I am not raising the score for effort -- my own independent read of this round's screenshots and measurements lands at the same place as round 2's for the same reason: the shell still leaves Lighthouse performance headroom on the table (below), which keeps this out of the 10 'clearly better, no nits' band, while everything else clears the 8.5 'equal to MDN/Real Python' anchor with room to spare given the total absence of anything comparable on the two top-ranking competing pages.
